sourceCheck: Checked on 2026-10-03. WCAG 2.2 is the W3C Recommendation dated 12 December 2024, first published 5 October 2023 and republished with errata. W3C's current overview identifies it as the latest WCAG 2.x Recommendation; WCAG 2.0 and 2.1 remain existing standards. WCAG 2.2 lists 4.1.1 Parsing as Obsolete and removed. Its current errata contain only editorial changes since republication, and the errata page was last modified 1 October 2026. WCAG 2.1 is the Recommendation dated 6 May 2025; it retains 4.1.1 Parsing at Level A with the HTML/XML always-satisfied note added by the 2023-04-18 erratum. WCAG 3.0 is a Working Draft dated 10 September 2026, not a Recommendation; WAI continues to advise meeting WCAG 2.2 now. WAI-ARIA 1.2 is the Recommendation dated 6 June 2023; WAI-ARIA 1.3 is a Working Draft dated 4 June 2026. ARIA in HTML is a Recommendation, current version 11 August 2026. HTML-AAM 1.0 is a Working Draft dated 23 September 2026. Accessible Name and Description Computation 1.2 is a Working Draft dated 2 October 2026. Using ARIA is a Discontinued Draft dated 24 February 2026 and is not a card source. MDN marks inert, :focus-visible, the dialog element and prefers-reduced-motion as Baseline Widely available, respectively since April 2023, March 2022, March 2022 and January 2020; this does not imply uniform support for newer subfeatures or assistive technologies. The requested section scopes support the planned facts. The known nested-header mapping disagreement remains: ARIA in HTML uses generic, while the HTML-AAM draft uses sectionheader. The corresponding card tests loss of the implicit banner mapping rather than asserting a replacement role. Draft-only ARIA features and the excluded MDN Understanding WCAG guides are not card sources. cards.statement: WCAG organizes its guidelines under perceivable, operable, understandable and robust.
cards.explanation: These principles organize accessibility needs across perception, interaction, understanding and compatibility with user agents, including assistive technology.

cards.statement: WCAG guidelines provide the pass-or-fail checks used to decide conformance.
cards.explanation: Success criteria provide the testable requirements. Guidelines state the broader goals rather than individual pass-or-fail checks.
cards.misconception: The guidelines themselves are the testable conformance requirements.

cards.statement: WCAG Level AA conformance requires meeting Level A as well as Level AA success criteria.
cards.explanation: Level AA builds on Level A; it is not a separate checklist that replaces the lower level.

cards.statement: WCAG permits authors to exclude an inaccessible sidebar when evaluating the rest of a page for conformance.
cards.explanation: Conformance applies to a complete page. Authors cannot declare a selected region conformant while excluding an inaccessible sidebar.
cards.misconception: A conforming main region makes the surrounding page conformant.

cards.statement: WCAG assesses conformance across the pages of a checkout process, including its payment step.
cards.explanation: Every page needed to complete a process must meet the target level. An accessible opening step does not cover a later nonconforming step.

cards.statement: WCAG allows a conforming alternate version to use a different technology from the original page.
cards.explanation: An alternate version may use different technology while providing equivalent information and functionality in the same language and staying equally current.

cards.statement: WCAG recommends Level AAA conformance as a general policy for entire websites.
cards.explanation: WCAG advises against a blanket Level AAA policy for entire sites because some content cannot satisfy every Level AAA success criterion.
cards.misconception: Level AAA is the recommended universal conformance target for whole websites.

cards.statement: The WCAG Techniques document prescribes the implementations developers use to achieve conformance.
cards.explanation: Techniques provide informative implementation options. Developers may use another approach that demonstrably meets the relevant success criteria.
cards.misconception: Conformance requires implementing one of the published Techniques.

source.title: Understanding Techniques for WCAG Success Criteria

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, a success criterion's position within its guideline indicates its conformance level.
cards.explanation: WCAG 2.2 appends new criteria to preserve existing numbering. The printed level, rather than position within the guideline, identifies the conformance level.
cards.misconception: Criteria remain ordered by conformance level within each guideline.

source.title: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2: Numbering in WCAG 2.2

cards.statement: Content that conforms to WCAG 2.2 also conforms to WCAG 2.1 and WCAG 2.0.
cards.explanation: W3C describes these versions as backwards compatible, so using WCAG 2.2 resources supports meeting the earlier versions too.

cards.statement: WCAG 3.0 has W3C Recommendation status alongside WCAG 2.2.
cards.explanation: WCAG 3.0 is a W3C Working Draft, not a completed Recommendation. Its draft status means the proposed requirements are still under development.
cards.misconception: The published WCAG 3.0 document is already a finalized W3C standard.
cards.volatilityNote: WCAG 3.0 may advance to a different publication status after this check.

cards.statement: The Accessibility Guidelines Working Group recommends WCAG 2.2 as a new conformance target.
cards.explanation: The working group recommends adopting WCAG 2.2 to benefit from its expanded accessibility requirements.
cards.volatilityNote: The recommended conformance target may change when W3C publishes a later standard.

source.title: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2: New Features in WCAG 2.2

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) (Level AA) permits a focused control to remain partly covered.
cards.explanation: Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) (Level AA) addresses author-created content that entirely hides a control receiving keyboard focus. Partial overlap is permitted.

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) belongs to the Level AA conformance requirements.
cards.explanation: Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) is Level AAA. Its enhanced protection is outside the requirements for a Level AA target.
cards.misconception: The enhanced focus-obscuring criterion is part of Level AA.

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, Focus Appearance (Level AAA) compares the same indicator pixels in focused and unfocused states.
cards.explanation: Focus Appearance (Level AAA) measures a 3:1 contrast change at the same pixels between states, rather than comparing the indicator with its adjacent color.

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, Dragging Movements (Level AA) accepts a keyboard shortcut as the alternative to dragging.
cards.explanation: Dragging Movements (Level AA) needs a non-dragging single-pointer route unless an exception applies. A keyboard shortcut alone does not provide that route.
cards.misconception: A keyboard alternative satisfies the pointer-specific dragging requirement.

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, Target Size (Minimum) (Level AA) includes a Spacing exception for undersized targets.
cards.explanation: For Target Size (Minimum) (Level AA), a 24 CSS pixel diameter circle centered on each undersized target's bounding box must avoid intersecting another target or another undersized target's circle.

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, Target Size (Minimum) (Level AA) applies its 24 by 24 CSS pixel minimum to links in sentences.
cards.explanation: Target Size (Minimum) (Level AA) exempts targets in sentences, or targets whose size is otherwise constrained by the line-height of non-target text.
cards.misconception: Inline links in prose are subject to the same minimum target dimensions as standalone controls.

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, Consistent Help (Level A) requires repeated help mechanisms to keep their relative page order.
cards.explanation: Consistent Help (Level A) concerns order relative to other content across a set of pages in the same page variation. User-initiated changes are excepted.

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, selecting an earlier checkout address satisfies Redundant Entry (Level A) for that repeated entry.
cards.explanation: Redundant Entry (Level A) permits selecting previously supplied information instead of typing it again within the same process.

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, Accessible Authentication (Minimum) (Level AA) accepts password-manager support as a mechanism.
cards.explanation: Accessible Authentication (Minimum) (Level AA) lists password-manager support as assistance that reduces memory demands during password entry.

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) (Level AAA) includes an Object Recognition exception.
cards.explanation: Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) (Level AAA) retains the Alternative and Mechanism exceptions. Object recognition is not an exception at this level.
cards.misconception: The enhanced authentication criterion exempts object-recognition tests.

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, the 44 by 44 CSS pixel criterion Target Size (Enhanced) forms part of Level AA conformance.
cards.explanation: Target Size (Enhanced) is Level AAA in WCAG 2.2. Its 44 by 44 CSS pixel threshold does not belong to a Level AA conformance target.
cards.misconception: The 44 by 44 CSS pixel target-size requirement is Level AA.

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, authors still assess 4.1.1 Parsing as a Level A requirement when reviewing HTML pages.
cards.explanation: WCAG 2.2 lists 4.1.1 Parsing as obsolete and removed. Assistive technology relies on browser parsing rather than parsing HTML itself.
cards.misconception: Parsing remains a current Level A requirement in WCAG 2.2.

cards.statement: Browsers build the accessibility tree from the DOM for use by assistive technology.
cards.explanation: The accessibility tree represents semantic information such as names, descriptions, roles and states, rather than being a visual copy of the page.

source.title: Accessibility tree - MDN Web Docs Glossary

cards.statement: Browsers give `Details` the implicit link role when exposing it to assistive technology.
cards.explanation: An `a` element needs `href` for its implicit link role. The shown markup has an implicit generic role.
cards.misconception: The anchor tag supplies link semantics even when its href attribute is absent.

cards.statement: A `<section aria-label="Details">` element exposes a region landmark to assistive technology.
cards.explanation: A section becomes a region landmark when it has an accessible name, allowing assistive technology to identify that page region.

source.title: ARIA: region role - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: A `<header>` inside an `<article>` supplies the document's implicit banner landmark.
cards.explanation: A header nested inside article content does not receive the implicit banner role. The banner mapping is for the page-level header, subject to the nesting restrictions.
cards.misconception: A header is a banner landmark regardless of its enclosing sectioning content.

source.title: ARIA: banner role - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: The `<search>` element gives its contents the semantics of an editable search input.
cards.explanation: The search element is a landmark container for search or filtering functionality. Authors place the actual input controls inside it.
cards.misconception: The search container has the semantics of a search input control.

source.title: <search>: The generic search element - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: The APG recommends different labels for navigation landmarks with different purposes.
cards.explanation: Distinct names help users distinguish navigation regions, such as primary navigation and links for the current section.

source.title: Landmark Regions - ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

cards.statement: Browsers derive a native heading's level from the depth of its surrounding `<section>` elements.
cards.explanation: A native heading gets its implicit level from the number in its h1–h6 tag. Nesting it in sections does not change that implicit level.
cards.misconception: The depth of section nesting determines the implicit accessibility level of a native heading.

source.title: HTML Accessibility API Mappings 1.0: h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, and h6

cards.statement: Meaningful Sequence (Level A) permits different reading orders that preserve the content's meaning.
cards.explanation: Meaningful Sequence (Level A) needs a correct reading order to be programmatically determinable when order affects meaning. Independent articles may support more than one correct order.

cards.statement: CSS allows authors to give a `<td>` cell table-header semantics by making its text bold.
cards.explanation: Bold styling changes appearance, not header semantics. The th element identifies a table header cell, with scope or explicit associations used where needed.
cards.misconception: Visual emphasis turns an ordinary data cell into a programmatically identified header.

source.title: <th>: The Table Header element - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: A `<caption>` inside a data table supplies a programmatically associated title for that table.
cards.explanation: The caption identifies its parent table and provides a table-specific title that assistive technology can use.

source.title: <caption>: The Table Caption element - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: Language of Page (Level A) requires a visible language selector on a single-language page.
cards.explanation: Language of Page (Level A) requires the default human language to be programmatically determinable, such as through lang="en" on html. A visible language selector is not required.
cards.misconception: Declaring a page's language requires offering a visible language selector.

cards.statement: Authors meet Page Titled (Level A) with document titles that identify the page's subject or function.
cards.explanation: Page Titled (Level A) helps users identify a page and distinguish it from other pages. In HTML, the document title belongs in the title element.

cards.statement: The markup `<button>Save</button>` supplies "Save" as the button's accessible name.
cards.explanation: A native button takes its accessible name from its content in this markup, making its displayed action text available as its name.

source.title: Providing Accessible Names and Descriptions - ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

cards.statement: For a button with valid `aria-labelledby` and `aria-label`, browsers use the `aria-label` value as its name.
cards.explanation: When aria-labelledby resolves to usable naming text, it takes precedence over aria-label. Supplying both does not give aria-label priority.
cards.misconception: A direct aria-label string outranks an aria-labelledby reference.

source.title: ARIA: aria-labelledby attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: A `<label>` element's `for` value links it to a form control's `name` attribute.
cards.explanation: An explicit HTML label associates through the control's id, matched by the label's for value. The control's name attribute is not the matching target.
cards.misconception: The label for value targets the control's form-submission name.

source.title: <label>: The Label element - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: In HTML-AAM, a text input's name falls back to `placeholder` after the earlier naming sources fail.
cards.explanation: HTML-AAM places placeholder after title in the text-input name computation. This specifies a fallback source rather than guaranteeing consistent spoken output.
cards.volatilityNote: HTML-AAM remains a Working Draft; this card tests its published computation, not universal assistive-technology behavior.

source.title: HTML Accessibility API Mappings 1.0: Text Input Accessible Name Computation

cards.statement: On a button, `aria-label` appends its text to the name supplied by the button's content.
cards.explanation: When aria-label supplies a button's name, its string replaces the content-derived name. The button's text is not automatically appended.
cards.misconception: aria-label supplements rather than replaces the button's content-derived name.

source.title: ARIA: aria-label attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: WAI-ARIA 1.2 permits `aria-label` to name a plain `<div>` with its implicit generic role.
cards.explanation: The generic role prohibits accessible naming. Adding aria-label to a plain div is not a valid way to name it under that role.
cards.misconception: aria-label is valid as a naming mechanism on elements with any implicit role.

source.title: ARIA: generic role - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: Authors use `aria-describedby` to associate supplementary instructions with a form control.
cards.explanation: aria-describedby references the IDs of elements containing descriptive text, such as format guidance that supplements a control's short name.

source.title: ARIA: aria-describedby attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: The APG recommends visible interface text as the first choice for an accessible name.
cards.explanation: The APG prioritizes names derived from visible text. Keeping naming text visible makes incorrect or stale labels easier to notice and maintain.

source.title: Providing Accessible Names and Descriptions - ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

cards.statement: The APG calls for translating `aria-label` strings along with the rest of a localized interface.
cards.explanation: aria-label contains human-readable naming text. The APG says these strings need translation alongside the rest of the interface.

source.title: Providing Accessible Names and Descriptions - ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

cards.statement: Link Purpose (In Context) (Level A) requires link text to explain its purpose independently of surrounding content.
cards.explanation: Link Purpose (In Context) (Level A) allows link text together with programmatically determined context to establish the purpose, such as the containing paragraph.
cards.misconception: Level A link purpose has to be clear from the isolated link text.

cards.statement: Headings and Labels (Level AA) evaluates semantic markup rather than the wording of headings.
cards.explanation: Headings and Labels (Level AA) evaluates whether headings and labels describe their topic or purpose. Correct semantic markup is a separate concern.
cards.misconception: This criterion tests structural markup instead of descriptive wording.

cards.statement: Label in Name (Level A) permits extra words around the visible label text in an accessible name.
cards.explanation: Label in Name (Level A) requires the name to contain the visible label text. Placing that text at the start is a best practice, not a requirement.
